rooms.about: This year we learn many spelling patterns so we can read new words on our own. We read stories and facts, write clear sentences, and share our ideas.

learn: Each vowel has a short sound: a as in cat, e as in bed, i as in pig, o as in hot, u as in sun.
A blend is two consonants side by side. You hear both sounds. In stop, you hear /s/ and /t/.
Some blends come at the start: bl, cr, fl, gr, sl, st, tr. Some come at the end: nd, st, mp, nk.
To read a word with a blend, say each sound and slide them together: f-r-o-g, frog.
units.try: Read these words out loud: flag, crab, step, hand, jump, trip. Point to the blend in each one. Then write two new words that start with st.
check: Which word starts with a blend?
What short vowel is in the word bed?

learn: A digraph is two letters that make one new sound.
Sh says /sh/ as in ship. Ch says /ch/ as in chin. Th says /th/ as in thumb.
Wh says /w/ as in when. Ck says /k/ at the end of short words, like duck and sock.
Digraphs can be at the start, middle, or end of a word: fish, lunch, bath.
units.try: Make a list of words with sh, ch, and th. Try: shop, wish, chip, much, thin, with. Circle the digraph in each. Read the list to a grown-up.
check: What sound does sh make in ship?

learn: Some words end with an e that you do not hear. We call it silent e or magic e.
Silent e makes the vowel before it say its own name. Cap becomes cape. Kit becomes kite.
The pattern is vowel, consonant, e. Look at hope, cube, and these.
Compare pairs to hear the change: hop and hope, tub and tube, pin and pine.
units.try: Write these words: can, hid, not, cut. Add an e to the end of each. Read the new words: cane, hide, note, cute. What changed in each one?
check: Add silent e to kit. What word do you get?
In the word home, what does the e do?
Makes the o say its name

learn: A vowel team is two vowels that work together to make one sound.
Ai and ay say long a: rain, play. Ee and ea often say long e: feet, seat.
Oa says long o: boat. Often the first vowel says its name and the second one is quiet.
Ay usually comes at the end of a word, like day. Ai usually comes in the middle, like tail.
units.try: Sort these words by sound: rain, tree, boat, day, read, road, sleep, mail. Make three groups: long a, long e, long o.
check: Which word has the long a sound?
What sound does oa make in boat?

learn: Good readers read smoothly, not word by word. This is called fluency.
Fluent readers know many sight words fast, like said, was, have, they, of, and come.
Read with expression. Make your voice sound like the character. Stop a little at a period.
Rereading a book helps. Each time you read it, it gets smoother.
units.try: Pick a short book or page. Read it out loud once. Then read it two more times. Ask a grown-up: Did it sound smoother the third time? Did I use expression?
check: What helps you read more smoothly?

learn: A noun names a person, place, thing, or animal. Mom, park, ball, and cat are nouns.
A proper noun names a special person or place. It starts with a capital letter, like Sam or Texas.
A verb is an action word. It tells what someone does. Run, eat, jump, and read are verbs.
Many nouns add s to mean more than one: one dog, two dogs. Some add es: box, boxes.
units.try: Look around the room. Name five nouns you see. Then act out five verbs, like hop, clap, sit, wave, and smile. Write one sentence with a noun and a verb: The dog runs.
check: What is the plural of box?

learn: A sentence is a complete thought. It tells who or what and what happens.
Start every sentence with a capital letter. The word I is always a capital letter.
End a telling sentence with a period. End a question with a question mark. End an excited sentence with an exclamation point.
Commas separate words in a list, like: I like red, blue, and green. Dates use commas too, like May 5, 2026.
units.try: Write three sentences about your day: one telling sentence, one question, and one excited sentence. Check each one for a capital letter and the right end mark.

learn: Stories have characters, a setting, and events. The main character is the one the story is mostly about.
Stories have a beginning, a middle, and an end. Often there is a problem, and by the end it is solved.
Good readers notice how characters feel and why. Look at the words and the pictures for clues.
A story often teaches a lesson. We call this the lesson or message of the story.
units.try: After reading a story, fold a paper into three parts. Draw the beginning, the middle, and the end. Under each picture, write one sentence about it.
check: What usually happens at the end of a story?
Where can you find clues about how a character feels?

learn: Informational books teach facts about a topic. The main topic is what the book is mostly about.
Text features help us find facts. A table of contents lists the parts of a book and their page numbers.
Headings tell what a section is about. Labels name the parts of a picture. A glossary explains hard words.
Good readers find key details. Key details are important facts that tell more about the topic.
units.try: Find an informational book. Use the table of contents to pick a section. Read it. Write the main topic and two key details you learned.
check: What does a table of contents show?
The parts of a book and page numbers
Names a part of a picture

learn: First graders write three kinds of pieces. An opinion piece tells what you think and why.
An informative piece teaches facts about a topic. A narrative tells a story about something that happened, in order.
Use order words in a story: first, next, then, last.
Writers plan, write, and then fix their work. Add details. Check capitals, spaces, and end marks.
units.try: Write an opinion piece. Start with: My favorite season is ___. Give two reasons using because. End with a closing sentence, like: That is why I love ___.
check: What kind of writing tells a true or made-up story in order?

rooms.about: This year we count to 120, understand tens and ones, and add and subtract within 20. We also measure, tell time, read graphs, and learn about shapes and equal parts.

learn: We can count to 120 starting at any number. After 99 comes 100, then 101, 102, and on to 120.
We can read and write these numbers. 107 means one hundred seven.
On a hundred chart, moving one box right adds 1. Moving one row down adds 10.
Skip counting by 2s, 5s, and 10s is a fast way to count groups.
units.try: Count on from 95 to 120 out loud. Then write the numbers 100 to 120 in two rows of ten and one more. Circle 110 and 120.

learn: Two-digit numbers are made of tens and ones. In 34, the 3 means 3 tens, or 30. The 4 means 4 ones.
Ten ones make one ten. We can bundle 10 sticks into one group of ten.
So 34 is 30 + 4. And 58 is 5 tens and 8 ones, or 50 + 8.
The numbers 10, 20, 30, up to 90 have tens and zero ones.
units.try: Show 46. Step 1: Make 4 bundles of 10 straws (or draw 4 long sticks). Step 2: Add 6 loose straws (or draw 6 dots). Step 3: Say it: 4 tens and 6 ones is 46. 40 + 6 = 46.
check: What number is 3 tens and 5 ones?

learn: To compare two-digit numbers, look at the tens first. 52 is more than 39 because 5 tens is more than 3 tens.
If the tens are the same, look at the ones. 47 is more than 43 because 7 ones is more than 3 ones.
We use symbols. > means greater than. < means less than. = means equal to.
The open side of > or < faces the bigger number. 61 > 16 and 16 < 61.
units.try: Compare 38 and 41. Step 1: Look at the tens. 38 has 3 tens. 41 has 4 tens. Step 2: 4 tens is more. Step 3: Write 38 < 41. The open side faces 41.

learn: There are many ways to add. You can count on from the bigger number. For 9 + 3, start at 9 and count 10, 11, 12.
Doubles are easy facts: 6 + 6 = 12. Near doubles use them: 6 + 7 is 6 + 6 + 1 = 13.
Making a ten helps. For 8 + 5, take 2 from the 5 to make 8 into 10. Then 10 + 3 = 13.
Order does not change the sum. 4 + 7 = 7 + 4 = 11. You can add three numbers too: 2 + 8 + 5 = 10 + 5 = 15.
units.try: Solve 9 + 6 by making ten. Step 1: 9 needs 1 more to make 10. Step 2: Take 1 from the 6. Now 6 is 5. Step 3: 10 + 5 = 15. So 9 + 6 = 15.

learn: Subtracting is taking away or finding the difference. 15 − 7 = 8.
You can count back. For 12 − 3, start at 12 and count back 11, 10, 9.
You can think addition. For 13 − 5, ask: 5 plus what makes 13? 5 + 8 = 13, so 13 − 5 = 8.
A fact family uses the same three numbers. 4 + 9 = 13, 9 + 4 = 13, 13 − 9 = 4, and 13 − 4 = 9.
units.try: Solve 14 − 6 by thinking addition. Step 1: Ask, 6 + ? = 14. Step 2: 6 + 4 = 10, and 10 + 4 = 14, so I added 8. Step 3: 14 − 6 = 8.
check: Which fact is in the same family as 3 + 8 = 11?

units.t: Word Problems and the Equal Sign
learn: Word problems tell a story with numbers. Read carefully. Ask: Are things being put together or taken away?
Words like in all and altogether often mean add. Words like left and how many more often mean subtract.
Draw a picture or use objects. Then write a number sentence.
The equal sign means both sides have the same value. 5 + 2 = 7 is true. 6 = 3 + 3 is also true.
units.try: Problem: Mia has 8 stickers. She gets 5 more. How many does she have in all? Step 1: In all means add. Step 2: 8 + 5. Step 3: 8 + 2 = 10, then 10 + 3 = 13. Answer: 13 stickers.
check: Ben had 12 grapes and ate 4. How many are left?

learn: Adding ten is easy. Ten more than 34 is 44. The tens digit goes up by 1. Ten less than 34 is 24.
To add tens to tens, add the tens. 30 + 40 = 70, like 3 tens + 4 tens = 7 tens.
To add a one-digit number to a two-digit number, add the ones. 42 + 5 = 47.
Sometimes the ones make a new ten. 36 + 7: 6 + 7 = 13, which is 1 ten and 3 ones. So 36 + 7 = 43.
units.try: Solve 28 + 6. Step 1: Add the ones: 8 + 6 = 14. Step 2: 14 is 1 ten and 4 ones. Step 3: 2 tens + 1 ten = 3 tens. Step 4: Answer: 34.

learn: Length is how long something is. To measure, lay same-size units end to end with no gaps or overlaps.
A pencil might be 6 paper clips long. We can order objects from shortest to longest.
A clock has a short hand for hours and a long hand for minutes. When the long hand points to 12, it is o'clock.
When the long hand points to 6, it is half past the hour. Half past 3 is written 3:30.
units.try: Measure a book with paper clips laid end to end. Count them. Then look at a clock with hands. At 2:00, the short hand is on 2 and the long hand on 12. Draw a clock for 7:30.
check: The short hand is on 4 and the long hand is on 12. What time is it?
When measuring with paper clips, what must you avoid?

learn: Data is information we collect, like the favorite fruits of a class.
We can sort data into groups, called categories. Then we count each group.
A tally mark is a quick way to count. Four lines with a slash across them makes 5.
A picture graph or bar graph shows data so we can compare. We can see which group has the most and how many more.
units.try: Ask 10 people their favorite color: red, blue, or green. Make tally marks. Draw a bar graph. Which color won? How many more votes did it get than the lowest?
check: Red got 6 votes and blue got 2. How many more votes did red get?
Four lines with a slash across stand for what number?

learn: Shapes have attributes. A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners. A rectangle has 4 sides and 4 square corners. Color and size do not change a shape.
We can put shapes together to make new shapes. Two triangles can make a square.
We can cut shapes into equal parts. Two equal parts are halves. Four equal parts are fourths, or quarters.
The more equal parts you cut, the smaller each part gets. A fourth of a pizza is smaller than a half.
units.try: Fold a paper square in half. Each part is one half. Now fold it in half again. Open it. You have 4 equal parts. Each part is one fourth. Color one fourth.
check: What do we call 2 equal parts of a whole?
Which piece of the same pizza is bigger?

rooms.about: This year we study sound and light, how plants and animals use their body parts, how young living things are like their parents, and patterns of the sun, moon, and stars.

learn: Sound is made when something vibrates. To vibrate means to move back and forth very fast.
When you pluck a rubber band, it vibrates and makes a sound. Touch your throat when you hum. You can feel it buzz.
Sound travels through air, water, and solid things to reach our ears.
Faster vibrations make higher sounds. Slower vibrations make lower sounds.
units.try: Stretch a rubber band around an open box. Pluck it and watch it vibrate. Then put rice on a drum or a pan lid. Tap the lid nearby gently. Watch the rice jump!

learn: We can only see things when there is light. Light comes from sources like the sun, lamps, and fire.
Light bounces off objects and goes into our eyes. That is how we see them.
In a completely dark room, we cannot see anything at all.
The moon does not make its own light. It reflects light from the sun.
units.try: Go into a dark closet with a grown-up. Can you see a toy in your hand? Now turn on a flashlight. What changed? Talk about why.
check: Can we see in a completely dark room?

learn: Light passes through some materials. Clear glass and plastic wrap are transparent. Light goes right through.
Some materials let only some light through, like wax paper. They are translucent.
Some materials block all light, like wood or cardboard. They are opaque. Opaque things make shadows.
A mirror is shiny and smooth. It reflects light, so it bounces light in a new direction.
units.try: Shine a flashlight through a clear cup, wax paper, and a book. Which one lets all the light through? Some? None? Then use a mirror to bounce light onto a wall.
check: What does a mirror do to light?

units.t: Sending Messages with Light and Sound
learn: People use light and sound to send messages far away.
A lighthouse shines light to warn ships of rocks. Traffic lights tell drivers to stop or go.
Fire alarms, sirens, and school bells use sound to tell us something important.
Long ago, people used drums and smoke signals to share news over long distances.
units.try: Make a secret code with a flashlight. One flash means yes. Two flashes mean no. Ask a family member questions and answer only with flashes.
check: Which uses sound to send a message?

learn: Plants have parts that help them live. Roots hold the plant in the ground and take in water.
The stem carries water up to the leaves and holds the plant up.
Leaves use sunlight to make food for the plant.
Flowers make seeds. Seeds grow into new plants. Some plants have thorns to keep animals from eating them.
units.try: Put a stalk of celery in a cup of water with a few drops of food coloring. Wait a day. Look at the leaves. The stem carried the colored water up!
check: Carries water and holds the plant up

learn: Animals have body parts that help them survive. Eagles have sharp eyes to spot food far away.
A duck has webbed feet for swimming. A giraffe has a long neck to reach high leaves.
A turtle's hard shell protects it. A porcupine has sharp quills.
Animals also act in ways that help them, like birds flying south in winter or bears sleeping through cold months.
units.try: Pick an animal. Draw it. Label two body parts and write how each one helps it find food, move, or stay safe.
check: How do webbed feet help a duck?

learn: People copy ideas from plants and animals to solve problems.
Burrs are seeds with tiny hooks that stick to fur. An inventor copied them to make hook-and-loop fasteners for shoes and bags.
Swim fins are like duck feet. Helmets are hard like a turtle's shell.
Some fast trains have long pointed fronts, shaped like a bird's beak. It helps them move quietly.
units.try: Design a coat to keep you warm, using an idea from an animal. Will it be thick like polar bear fur? Draw it and label the animal idea.
check: Swim fins copy what animal part?
Burrs gave people the idea for what?

learn: Young animals and plants look like their parents in many ways. A kitten looks like a cat.
Young ones are not exactly the same as their parents. Puppies in one litter can have different colors.
Some young animals change a lot as they grow. A tadpole becomes a frog. A caterpillar becomes a butterfly.
Many animal parents care for their young. Birds feed their chicks. Some animals hide or carry their babies.
units.try: Look at baby photos of yourself and your family. How do you look like your family? How are you different? Draw a parent animal and its baby side by side.
check: What does a tadpole grow into?
Are puppies always exactly like their parents?

learn: The sun seems to rise in the east in the morning and set in the west at night. This happens because Earth spins.
We see stars at night. During the day, the sun is so bright we can't see other stars.
The moon seems to change shape. We call these shapes phases. The full pattern takes about one month.
We see a full moon when the whole round side is lit. A new moon is when we can't see it at all.
units.try: For one week, look at the moon each evening with a grown-up. Draw its shape each night. Does it look bigger or smaller as the days go by?
check: Where does the sun seem to rise?
Why can't we see stars in the daytime?

learn: The amount of daylight changes during the year.
In summer, days are long. The sun rises early and sets late.
In winter, days are short. It may be dark when you wake up or before dinner.
In spring and fall, day and night are closer to the same length. This pattern repeats every year.
units.try: Ask a grown-up to help you find the sunrise and sunset times for today. Then find them for a day in summer and a day in winter. Which day has the most daylight?
check: Does the daylight pattern repeat each year?

rooms.about: This year we learn about communities, rules and leaders, maps and land, the past and present, goods and services, money, and American symbols and holidays.

learn: A community is a group of people who live, work, and play in one area.
Communities can be big or small. A city has many people and tall buildings. A town or farm area has fewer people and more open land.
Suburbs are places near cities with many homes and yards.
Communities have places we share, like schools, libraries, parks, and hospitals.
units.try: Take a walk or drive with a grown-up. List five places in your community, like a store, a park, or a library. Draw a map of the route you took.
check: Which community usually has the most people?
A shared place to borrow books

learn: Rules are for a home, school, or game. Laws are rules for a whole community, state, or country.
Laws keep people safe. Speed limits, seat belt laws, and no littering are laws.
Rules and laws should be fair. They should be the same for everyone.
If people break a law, there are consequences, like paying a fine.
units.try: Look for signs near your home. Find a stop sign, a speed limit sign, or a no-parking sign. Tell what law the sign shows and how it keeps people safe.

learn: A leader helps a group make decisions and solve problems.
A principal leads a school. A mayor leads a city or town. A governor leads a state.
The President leads the United States. In the U.S., grown-up citizens vote to choose many leaders.
To vote means to make a choice. The choice with the most votes wins.
units.try: Hold a family vote. Choose two dinner ideas or two games. Everyone votes once. Count the votes. The one with the most wins. Was it fair?
check: What does it mean to vote?

learn: A map shows a place from above. A map key, or legend, tells what each symbol means.
A compass rose shows directions: north, south, east, and west.
On most maps, north is at the top. South is at the bottom. East is right. West is left.
Maps help us find our way. We can make maps of a room, a school, or a neighborhood.
units.try: Draw a map of your street or yard. Make a map key with symbols: a small square for houses, a green circle for trees. Add a compass rose with N, S, E, W.
check: On most maps, which direction is at the top?
What does a map key tell you?

learn: Earth has seven continents: North America, South America, Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia, and Antarctica.
Earth has five oceans: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, and Southern. The Pacific is the biggest.
Land has many forms. Mountains are very high. Plains are flat. Islands have water all around them.
Water has many forms too. Rivers flow across land. Lakes have land all around them.
units.try: Look at a world map or globe. Find North America, where the United States is. Find the Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean. Which ocean is on each side of the U.S.?
check: Land with water all around it
Water with land all around it

learn: The past is before now. The present is now. The future is what will come.
A timeline shows events in order. The oldest events go first, on the left.
We use words like yesterday, today, and tomorrow, and before, now, and later.
Calendars show days, weeks, and months. There are 7 days in a week and 12 months in a year.
units.try: Make a timeline of your life. Draw yourself as a baby, learning to walk, starting kindergarten, and now in first grade. Put them in order from left to right.
check: How many months are in a year?
On a timeline, where do the oldest events go?

learn: Life long ago was different from today. Many families grew their own food and made their own clothes.
Many children helped with chores, like carrying water, feeding animals, and gathering wood.
Many children walked to school. Some went to a one-room schoolhouse where all ages learned together.
Some things are the same. Families still eat together, play games, celebrate, and help each other.
units.try: Make a then-and-now chart. On one side, draw how people did something long ago, like washing clothes by hand. On the other side, draw how we do it today.
check: A school where all ages learned together
What is still the same today?

learn: Goods are things people make or grow, like apples, shoes, and toys.
Services are jobs people do for others, like cutting hair, teaching, or fixing cars.
Producers make goods or give services. Consumers buy and use them. Everyone is a consumer.
People in a community depend on each other. A baker needs a farmer for flour.
units.try: Look around your kitchen. Find three goods. Then name three people who give your family services, like a doctor or a bus driver. Who are the producers?
check: Someone who buys and uses goods or services

learn: People earn money by working. They use money to buy goods and services.
U.S. coins include the penny (1 cent), nickel (5 cents), dime (10 cents), and quarter (25 cents).
Saving means keeping money to use later. Spending means using money to buy things now.
We can't buy everything, so we choose. Needs come before wants.
units.try: Sort real or play coins into piles: pennies, nickels, dimes, and quarters. Which coin is worth the most? Then plan: if you had 10 dollars, how much would you save?
check: How much is a dime worth?

learn: The American flag has 13 stripes and 50 stars. The bald eagle and the Liberty Bell are national symbols.
Independence Day is July 4. It marks the Declaration of Independence in 1776.
Martin Luther King Jr. Day honors a leader who worked peacefully for equal rights for Black Americans and all people.
Thanksgiving is a day to give thanks. Veterans Day honors people who served in the military.
units.try: Make a holiday calendar. Write the name of each month. Add Independence Day, Thanksgiving, and Martin Luther King Jr. Day in the right months. Add one family holiday too.
check: In what year was the Declaration of Independence signed?
Who does Martin Luther King Jr. Day honor?
A leader who worked for equal rights

rooms.about: This year we use the elements of art: line, shape, color, texture, and space. We paint, print, build, and learn about art from around the world.

learn: Artists use many kinds of lines: straight, curved, zigzag, wavy, dotted, and spiral.
Lines can go in different directions. Horizontal lines lie flat like the ground. Vertical lines stand up tall like a tree. Diagonal lines slant.
Horizontal lines can feel calm. Diagonal lines can feel like motion, like rain in the wind.
An outline is a line around the edge of a shape.
units.try: Draw a picture of a windy day using only lines. Use horizontal lines for the ground, vertical lines for trees, and diagonal lines for rain blowing sideways.
check: Which line stands up tall like a tree?
Which kind of line can show motion?

learn: A shape is a flat, closed area. It has height and width.
Geometric shapes have neat edges, like circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles. Many are found in buildings.
Organic shapes are free and curvy. They come from nature, like puddles, clouds, and leaves.
Artists mix both kinds of shapes in their work.
units.try: Make two pictures. In one, draw a city using only geometric shapes. In the other, draw a garden using only organic shapes. Which feels busier? Which feels softer?
check: Where do we often see geometric shapes?

learn: A color wheel shows how colors relate. The primary colors are red, yellow, and blue.
Secondary colors are made by mixing two primaries: orange (red + yellow), green (yellow + blue), and purple (blue + red).
On the color wheel, each secondary color sits between the two colors that make it.
Black and white are not on the basic wheel, but they change colors. White makes a tint. Black makes a shade.
units.try: Paint or color a simple color wheel. Draw a circle and cut it into six parts like a pizza. Color red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple in that order around the circle.

learn: Colors can feel warm or cool.
Warm colors are red, orange, and yellow. They remind us of fire and the sun. They can feel exciting.
Cool colors are blue, green, and purple. They remind us of water, grass, and ice. They can feel calm.
Artists choose warm or cool colors to set a mood in their art.
units.try: Draw the same tree twice. Color one with only warm colors, like a sunset. Color the other with only cool colors, like a night. How does each one feel?
check: Cool colors often remind us of what?

units.t: Texture You Can See and Touch
learn: Real texture is what you feel when you touch something, like the bumps on a basket.
Visual texture is texture that is drawn. It only looks bumpy or furry. The paper is still flat.
Artists draw texture with marks: short lines for fur, dots for sand, scales for a fish.
Adding real things like yarn, sand, or fabric to a picture gives it real texture.
units.try: Draw an animal, like a sheep or a hedgehog. Show texture: use curly lines for wool or short spiky lines for spines. Then glue a few cotton balls or yarn pieces on for real texture.

learn: A pattern is made when lines, shapes, or colors repeat in a planned way.
A simple pattern is AB, like circle, square, circle, square. An ABC pattern has three parts.
Patterns show up in nature, like stripes on a tiger or rings in a tree.
Many cultures use patterns in quilts, weaving, pottery, and clothes.
units.try: Make a paper weaving. Cut slits in one paper, leaving a border. Weave strips of another color over and under. You will make a checkerboard pattern.
check: What comes next: circle, square, triangle, circle, square, ...?
Where do we find patterns in nature?

learn: Space in art is the area around and between things.
Things that are near look bigger. Things that are far away look smaller.
Things lower on the page look closer. Things higher on the page look farther away.
Overlapping means one thing is in front of another. The thing in front looks closer.
units.try: Draw a landscape. Put a big tree low on the page. Put a small house higher up. Draw mountains at the top, behind the house so they overlap. Does it look deep?
check: Things far away in a picture look how?
One thing in front of another

learn: A print is made by pressing an inked or painted surface onto paper.
You can make many copies of the same print. That is what makes printmaking special.
Stamps can be made from sponges, foam, or even vegetables like potato halves cut by a grown-up.
A print shows the design flipped, like a mirror image.
units.try: With a grown-up's help, cut a sponge into a shape. Dip it in paint. Press it on paper. Lift it up. Repeat to make a pattern of prints.
check: How does a print show the design?

learn: A shape is flat. A form is 3D. Forms have height, width, and depth.
A sphere is a ball form. A cube is a box form. A cylinder is a can form.
Sculptors make forms with clay, paper, wood, metal, or recycled materials.
Two ways to make clay pieces stick together are scoring and smoothing. Scratch both sides, then press and smooth.
units.try: Build a sculpture from recycled things: boxes, tubes, and lids. Tape them together to make a robot, a castle, or an animal. Paint it if you like.
check: What does a form have that a shape does not?

learn: People everywhere make art. Art can show beliefs, stories, and everyday life.
Some cultures make pottery, masks, weaving, or carvings. Many Native American nations make beadwork and baskets.
Some art is very old, like cave paintings that are thousands of years old.
When we look at art, we describe what we see, think about how it was made, and share how it makes us feel.
units.try: Look at a picture of art from another culture in a book. Describe it: What colors, lines, and shapes do you see? Then make your own art inspired by it.
check: What is a good first step when looking at art?
How old are some cave paintings?

rooms.about: This year we learn beat and rhythm, reading simple notes, melody, dynamics, tempo, instrument families, and song form. We sing, play, and listen to music from many places.

learn: The beat is the steady pulse of music. It never stops or changes speed unless the music tells it to.
Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds that goes with the beat. The words of a song make a rhythm.
Some beats feel stronger. In a march, it goes STRONG, weak, STRONG, weak.
We can keep the beat with our feet while we clap the rhythm with our hands.
units.try: Sing a song like Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star. First, pat the steady beat on your knees. Then clap the rhythm of the words. Do they sound different?
check: What is the steady pulse in music?

learn: Musicians write rhythm with notes. A quarter note gets one beat. We say ta.
Two eighth notes share one beat. They are joined by a beam. We say ti-ti.
A quarter rest means one beat of silence. We show it by staying quiet.
We can read patterns like ta, ta, ti-ti, ta. That is four beats.
units.try: Clap and say this pattern: ta, ti-ti, ta, rest. On the rest, open your hands and stay silent. Then make up your own four-beat pattern and teach it to someone.
check: How many beats does a quarter note get?

learn: A melody is a line of notes that goes up and down. It is the tune you hum.
Notes can move up, move down, or stay the same.
A step is a move to the next note. A leap jumps over notes.
Melodies can be drawn as lines. A line going up means the notes go higher.
units.try: Sing a song you know slowly. Move your hand up when the notes go up and down when they go down. Then draw the melody as a wavy line on paper.
check: A line of notes going up and down

learn: Musicians give notes names to help sing them. Two easy notes are sol and mi.
Sol is higher. Mi is lower. Many playground songs use them, like the calls in a game of tag.
Some teachers show notes with hand signs. The sign for sol is held higher, and the sign for mi is held lower.
Later we add la, which is just above sol, to make more songs.
units.try: Sing sol-mi, sol-mi, like a call: Hel-lo! Then sing your name on sol and mi. Use a hand sign: high hand for sol, low hand for mi.
check: Which note is just above sol?

learn: Dynamics tell how loud or soft to play or sing.
Musicians use Italian words. Piano means soft. Forte means loud.
We write them with letters: p for piano and f for forte.
Music can get louder little by little. That is called crescendo. Getting softer is decrescendo.
units.try: Sing a song softly (piano). Then sing it loudly (forte). Then start soft and slowly get louder for a crescendo. Show it with your hands moving apart.

learn: Tempo is the speed of the beat.
Allegro means fast. Largo means very slow. Moderato means medium.
Music can speed up. That is accelerando. It can slow down. That is ritardando.
The tempo helps set the mood. A lullaby is slow. A chase scene in a movie is fast.
units.try: Clap a steady beat while a grown-up calls out allegro, moderato, or largo. Change your speed each time. Then try speeding up slowly from largo to allegro.

learn: Instruments are grouped into families by how they make sound.
Strings, like violin and cello, make sound when strings vibrate. Woodwinds, like the flute and clarinet, use air blown through a tube.
Brass instruments, like the trumpet and tuba, buzz with the player's lips.
Percussion instruments, like drums and xylophones, are struck, shaken, or scraped. The piano is often called a percussion and string instrument.
units.try: Listen to a short piece of orchestra music. Raise your hand when you hear a drum. Wave when you hear a violin. Sort a list of instruments into the four families.
check: Which family does the trumpet belong to?
How do string instruments make sound?

learn: Form is the plan of a piece of music. It tells which parts repeat and which are different.
We name parts with letters. If a song has two different parts, it is AB form.
If the first part comes back at the end, it is ABA form.
Call and response is a form too. A leader sings a call. The group sings a response.
units.try: Make an ABA dance. For part A, clap to the music. For part B, march. Then go back to clapping for A. Use any song you like and switch when the music changes.
check: A part, a new part, then the first part again
What happens in call and response?
A leader sings, then the group answers

learn: Good posture helps you sing. Stand or sit tall with your shoulders relaxed and feet flat.
Take a low, deep breath before you sing. Your belly should move out, not your shoulders up.
Open your mouth wide enough for sound to come out. Sing gently. Don't shout.
Match the pitch. Listen to the note, then sing the same note.
units.try: Stand tall. Place your hand on your belly. Breathe in slowly and feel it move out. Then sing one note on oo for as long as you can. Do this three times.
check: When you breathe in to sing, what should move?

learn: Every culture has music. People sing at celebrations, at work, and to tell stories.
Some instruments come from special places. The steel pan comes from Trinidad and Tobago. The sitar comes from India.
Many songs in other languages have the same feelings as ours: joy, love, and fun.
Folk songs are passed down from parent to child for many years.
units.try: Ask a family member to teach you a song they learned as a child. Learn it, sing it together, and talk about where it came from.
check: Where does the steel pan come from?
A song passed down for many years
A song with no words ever

rooms.about: This year we practice moving, jumping, throwing, catching, and kicking. We learn how exercise helps our heart, how to eat well, stay clean, handle feelings, and stay safe.

learn: A warm-up gets your body ready to move. It makes muscles warm and loose.
Start slowly. March in place, swing your arms, and do gentle stretches.
Keep your personal space. Look where you're going so you don't bump into others.
Wear shoes that fit and are tied. Drink water when you're active.
units.try: Do this warm-up: march in place for 30 seconds, do 10 arm circles forward and 10 backward, then reach up high and down to your toes 5 times.
check: To get our body ready to move
What should you drink when you're active?

learn: Locomotor skills move you from place to place: walk, run, hop, jump, gallop, slide, leap, and skip.
A slide is sideways steps, like a crab. A leap is a long step from one foot to the other, flying through the air.
You can move in different directions: forward, backward, and sideways.
You can move at different levels: low like a crawl, middle, or high on your tiptoes.
units.try: Play follow-the-leader with a family member. Take turns choosing a move: skip, slide, gallop, leap. Add a direction (backward!) and a level (low!).
check: A long step from one foot to the other

learn: To jump far, bend your knees, swing your arms back, then swing them forward as you jump.
Land softly on both feet with your knees bent. This protects your joints.
A jump for height goes up. A jump for distance goes forward.
Jumping rope is great exercise. Start by jumping over a rope on the ground.
units.try: Put a sock on the floor as a starting line. Do a standing long jump. Bend, swing, jump, land softly. Mark where your heels land. Try three times. Did you go farther?
check: How should you land after a jump?

learn: For an underhand throw, face your target, swing your arm back, step with the opposite foot, and swing forward and release.
For an overhand throw, turn your side to the target, bring the ball back by your ear, step, and throw.
To catch a high ball, thumbs together. To catch a low ball, pinkies together.
Watch the ball all the way into your hands. Give with your arms to soften the catch.
units.try: With a partner and a soft ball, practice 10 underhand throws and 10 overhand throws. Say thumbs or pinkies before each catch, depending on how high it comes.
check: To catch a low ball, what should touch?
For an overhand throw, where does the ball start?

learn: To kick a ball, put your non-kicking foot beside the ball. Swing your kicking leg and hit the ball with your laces.
For a short, careful pass, use the inside of your foot.
Dribbling with your feet means tapping the ball gently as you walk or jog, keeping it close.
Keep your eyes up some of the time so you can see where you are going.
units.try: Set up two cups or shoes as a goal. Dribble a ball across the yard with small taps. Stop and pass it into the goal with the inside of your foot.
check: Which part of the foot is best for a short pass?
What does dribbling with your feet mean?
Tapping the ball gently while moving
Kicking it as hard as you can

learn: Your heart is a muscle. It pumps blood all through your body.
Exercise makes your heart stronger. Running, swimming, biking, and dancing all help.
Kids should be active for at least 60 minutes each day.
Strong muscles help you lift, climb, and play. Push-ups, climbing, and jumping build muscles. Stretching keeps you flexible.
units.try: Find your pulse on your wrist or neck with a grown-up's help. Count beats for 10 seconds. Then do 30 seconds of fast jumping. Count again. What happened?
check: How long should kids be active each day?

learn: Food is fuel for your body. The five food groups are fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, and dairy.
Fill half your plate with fruits and vegetables. Whole grains like oatmeal and brown rice give lasting energy.
Protein, like beans, eggs, fish, and chicken, helps build muscles.
Water is the best drink. Sugary drinks and candy are sometimes foods, not everyday foods.
units.try: Help make a healthy snack with a grown-up, like apple slices with cheese or carrot sticks with hummus. Name the food group of each part.
check: Which food group are beans in?
How much of your plate should be fruits and vegetables?

learn: Germs spread on hands, through coughs, and by sharing cups. Clean habits help stop them.
Wash hands with soap for 20 seconds. Cover coughs and sneezes with your elbow.
Take baths or showers to keep your body clean. Wash your hair too.
Don't share cups, spoons, or hats. Keep your fingers out of your mouth, nose, and eyes.
units.try: Put a little glitter or flour on your hands to pretend it is germs. Shake hands with a grown-up. See how it spreads? Now wash it all off with soap and water.

learn: Everyone has many feelings each day. Naming a feeling helps. Say: I feel frustrated.
Calm-down tools include deep breaths, counting, drawing, or taking a short break.
Good friends take turns, share, include others, and say sorry when they make a mistake.
Bullying is when someone keeps hurting or picking on another person on purpose. If you see it, tell a trusted adult.
units.try: Play the feelings face game. A grown-up makes a face. You guess the feeling. Then switch. Talk about a time you felt that way and what helped.
check: What should you do if you see bullying?

learn: Fire safety: stop, drop, and roll if your clothes catch fire. Crawl low under smoke. Never play with matches or lighters.
Know two ways out of every room. Have a family meeting place outside.
Wear a helmet on bikes and scooters. Buckle up in the car, and ride in the back seat.
Water safety: only swim when an adult is watching. Wear a life jacket on a boat.
units.try: Plan a fire escape with your family. Walk two ways out of your bedroom. Choose a meeting spot outside, like a big tree or a neighbor's mailbox. Practice once.
check: What do you do if your clothes catch fire?
Only when an adult is watching
